newsitem.title: UK: UK government tackles tax avoidance loopholes.
newsitem.headline: UK government tackles tax avoidance loopholes.

text.p: The British government moved on Wednesday to close a couple of loopholes open to tax avoiders.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke tabled two clauses to be added to the Finance Bill, currently going through parliament, the first of which is aimed at stopping the use of artificial derivatives transactions for tax avoidance purposes.
Angela Knight, Economic Secretary to the Treasury, said tax shirkers can use such schemes to turn interest income into capital gains, and thereby pay less tax.

"There is evidence of growing use of these schemes, so immediate action is needed to prevent further tax loss," she said. "The new clause will counter tax avoidance schemes which use options or futures to convert income into capital gains."
The second clause will tackle companies which carry on life assurance business of artificial annuities for tax avoidance purposes.

A complicated loophole was explained by Financial Secretary to the Treasury Michael Jack. "Evidence has come to light that major financial institutions have sought to exploit the rules for determining how much of a life annuity is income," he said.
As with the first scam, a higher rate of tax is paid on income rather than capital.

Jack said a bank or other financial house could take out a large life assurance annuity or a series of annuities, made up in such a way that the income element on which tax relief is claimed by the life insurer that wrote the policy is much larger than the economic income return inherent in the annuity.

"The arrangement involves making substantial payments for a short period followed by a lengthy period when a trivial payment is made," Jack said. "If unchecked, use of such annuity arrangements could lead to the erosion of the entire tax base of life assurance companies."
Both clauses will be introduced at the "Report Stage" of the Finance Bill, which when it has passed through parliament, will make law Clarke's proposals at last November's budget.
